content: Paronychia is an infection of the skin that occurs around the nails. It typically presents as a painful, red, and swollen area near the nail, often at the cuticle or where a hangnail or other injury has occurred. In cases of bacterial infection, pus-filled blisters may develop, and the condition tends to appear suddenly. If the infection is caused by a fungus, it usually progresses more slowly. Changes to the nail may also occur, such as detachment, abnormal shape, or discoloration. Paronychia is commonly caused by trauma to the area, such as biting or picking at a hangnail, trimming or pushing back the cuticle, or other forms of injury. Bacterial paronychia is caused by bacteria, while candidal paronychia is caused by a specific type of yeast. Fungal paronychia results from a fungal infection. In some cases, both bacterial and fungal infections may coexist. Individuals at higher risk for fungal paronychia include those with pre-existing fungal nail infections, people with diabetes, and individuals who frequently immerse their hands in water for extended periods. It is important to seek medical attention if symptoms persist despite treatment, worsen, or if new symptoms develop. These symptoms may include chills, fever, red streaks along the skin, a general feeling of being unwell, joint pain, muscle pain, or the local spread of the infection. A healthcare provider can typically diagnose paronychia by examining the affected area. If necessary, pus or fluid from the site may be drained and sent to a laboratory to identify the specific bacteria or fungus responsible for the infection. Treatment for bacterial paronychia often involves soaking the affected nail in warm water two to three times daily to reduce swelling and pain. Antibiotics may be prescribed, and in severe cases, the doctor may need to drain the infected area or remove part of the nail. For fungal paronychia, antifungal medications are typically prescribed. Patients are advised to keep their hands dry and may use a skin-drying agent, such as Castellani's paint. Paronychia generally responds well to treatment, although fungal infections may persist for several months. Complications are rare but can include abscess formation, permanent nail deformities, or the spread of infection to deeper tissues, such as tendons, bones, or the bloodstream. To protect nails from damage, individuals should use protective gloves when handling detergents or chemicals and bring their own manicure tools to nail salons. Nails should be trimmed weekly, with toenails trimmed monthly. Fingernails should be cut with a slightly rounded edge, while toenails should be trimmed straight across. Cuticles should not be trimmed or removed, as this can damage the skin and create an entry point for bacteria or fungi, increasing the risk of infection.
